sets.title: Sleep and memory
sets.transcript: We used to think of sleep as a kind of switching off, a period when the brain simply rests. We now know that's far from the truth. During deep sleep, the brain replays what we learned during the day, and moves those memories from short-term storage into long-term storage. In one well-known experiment, students who slept after learning a list of words remembered significantly more the next day than students who stayed awake for the same length of time. So, if you're studying a language, the evening review is especially valuable. Go over your new vocabulary before bed, and let your brain do the rest. What doesn't work, unfortunately, is staying up all night before an exam; you may gain a few hours of study, but you lose the very process that makes it stick.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say about the old view of sleep?
options: It was wrong to see sleep as simply switching off.
questions.explain: “We used to think of sleep as a kind of switching off… We now know that's far from the truth.”

options: Memories move from short-term to long-term storage.
questions.explain: “…moves those memories from short-term storage into long-term storage.”

options: Students who slept remembered more words.
Students who stayed awake remembered more words.
questions.explain: “Students who slept after learning… remembered significantly more the next day.”

questions.prompt: What does the speaker recommend for language learners?
questions.explain: “Go over your new vocabulary before bed, and let your brain do the rest.”

options: You lose the process that makes learning stick.

questions.explain: “You may gain a few hours of study, but you lose the very process that makes it stick.”
